column11: How does ascending pelvic inflammatory disease progress from endometritis to tubo-ovarian abscess, and why does the imaging anatomy become progressively less distinct?
column12: Infection damages the endocervical barrier and ascends to the endometrium, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and peritoneal cavity. Tubal inflammation can obstruct the lumen and trap infected material, producing pyosalpinx; ovarian involvement produces oophoritis. Progressive inflammation and adhesions then bind the tube and ovary into a tubo-ovarian complex and, with further destructive infection, an inseparable tubo-ovarian abscess. Imaging follows that chain: endometrial fluid/enhancement -> thickened hyperemic tube with complex fluid -> enlarged inflamed ovary -> loss of separable tubo-ovarian anatomy in TOA.

column11: Why do active salpingitis and pyosalpinx produce the cogwheel appearance and incomplete septa on ultrasound?
column12: The source links the cogwheel appearance to thickening of the longitudinal endosalpingeal folds. When an inflamed fallopian tube dilates and folds on itself, those thickened folds become nodular internal projections and the folded tubular lumen can simulate incomplete septa. The imaging pivot is therefore tubular microanatomy: a tortuous inflamed tube with thickened endosalpingeal folds can look internally septated without being a true multilocular ovarian cyst.

🔍 Key Imaging Findings
  • PID spans endometritis, salpingitis, pyosalpinx, oophoritis, tubo-ovarian complex, TOA, peritonitis, and Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome.
  • TOC: abscess/inflammatory material is adherent to the tube but the ovary remains distinguishable. TOA: tube and ovary are involved together and the separate ovary is no longer recognizable.
  • US: thickened dilated tube, complex fluid, low-level debris, fluid-debris levels, incomplete septa from a folded tube, cogwheel appearance from thickened endosalpingeal folds, wall often at least 5 mm, hyperemia, and probe tenderness.
  • CT: pelvic fat stranding/haziness, obscured planes, free fluid, peritoneal enhancement, thickened/enhancing tubes, enlarged enhancing ovaries, uterine/endometrial inflammatory change, and thick-walled complex collections in advanced disease.
  • MR: T1 low/intermediate fluid with possible hemorrhagic/proteinaceous/purulent hyperintensity, T2 intermediate-to-high fluid, thick irregular walls/septa, parametrial edema, rim/septal/peritoneal enhancement, and often high DWI with low ADC.

⚖️ Differential Diagnosis
  • Endometrioma may show T1 hyperintensity, T2 shading, and diffusion restriction; less infectious fat stranding and endometriosis context favor endometrioma.
  • Hemorrhagic ovarian cyst is usually a single thin-walled ovarian cyst without thick inflamed tube or pelvic fat inflammation.
  • Hydrosalpinx has simple tubal fluid without wall thickening or surrounding inflammation; hematosalpinx is avascular blood-filled tube often clarified on MR.
  • Appendicitis, diverticulitis, Crohn disease, torsion, dermoid, ovarian neoplasm, ectopic pregnancy, and paraovarian cyst are important mimics; trace the inflammatory epicenter.

🚩 Complications / Spread
  • TOA rupture can cause life-threatening peritonitis. Other complications include pelvic abscess, bowel ileus/obstruction, reactive bowel or bladder change, ureteral obstruction, thrombophlebitis/ovarian vein thrombosis, adhesions, and chronic tubal damage.
  • Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is perihepatitis from spread through the right paracolic gutter; CT/MR may show anterior hepatic capsular enhancement, subcapsular/periportal perfusion change, periportal edema, gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, right paracolic gutter stranding, or loculated perihepatic fluid.

🩻 Clinical / Management
  • Most PID is ascending infection, commonly Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis, but many cases are polymicrobial and secondary spread from appendicitis/diverticulitis/colitis can occur.
  • Transvaginal US is first line. CT helps when symptoms are nonspecific, complications or nongynecologic mimics are possible, or drainage planning is needed. MR helps when US/CT are equivocal or TOA must be separated from other ovarian masses.
  • TOA may require hospitalization, parenteral antibiotics, image-guided drainage, or surgery for poor response, large/accessible abscess, rupture, generalized peritonitis, septic shock, or uncertain diagnosis.
